findings.issue: No Western Front or occupation position before 20 August: the invasion of Luxembourg (2 Aug) and Belgium (4 Aug) and the fall of Liège (7 Aug) never appeared; the chapter's first half showed an empty map. Added keys on 4 and 12 August (Luxembourg occupied, Germans to Liège and the Gete).

Only two positions (20 Aug, 5 Sep) for the whole German advance, so Mons (23 Aug), the fall of Namur (25 Aug), Le Cateau (26 Aug) and the drive past Amiens (31 Aug) slid by in one straight interpolation. Added keys on 24 and 30 August.

The French offensives into Lorraine (Sarrebourg, 18 Aug) and Alsace (Mulhouse retaken 19 Aug) were missing, and so was the German capture of Lunéville and St-Dié afterwards. The 20 August front now bulges into Lorraine, a new French-held Alsace area shows Mulhouse (19–24 Aug) and the Thann strip France kept all war, and the late-August line runs behind Lunéville until it was retaken on 13 September.

The German Schlieffen arrow stopped at Meaux; Kluck's First Army crossed the Marne on 3 September and reached the Grand Morin. Path re-routed through Liège, Brussels, Mons and Le Cateau to end south of the Marne.

source.title: Wikipedia: First Battle of the Marne

findings.issue: The besieged fortresses of Maubeuge (to 7 Sep) and Givet (to 31 Aug) sit inside the German area on 30 Aug and 5 Sep; occupied areas are single rings and cannot hold Allied pockets. Left as is.

Western Front had no position from 5 September to 15 December: the Aisne line (13–14 Sep), the St-Mihiel salient (24 Sep), the Race to the Sea (Roye, Albert, Arras, Lens, 22 Sep–8 Oct), the fall of Antwerp (10 Oct) and Lille (13 Oct), the Yser line (15 Oct) and First Ypres were all missing. Added keys on 14 and 26 Sep, 7, 16 and 31 Oct and 22 Nov.

findings.issue: Between 5 Sep and 15 Dec the map interpolated Antwerp and Ghent slowly into German hands and showed the Ypres line through ground the Germans never reached in September; Antwerp now stays Belgian until 10 October and Lille French until 13 October.

Text said the trenches ran from the 'Channel coast'; the line began at Nieuwpoort on the Belgian North Sea coast. Text rewritten (also names the fall of Antwerp and the defence of Ypres, the chapter's main events).

The German-occupied area's northern edge used points inside the neutral Netherlands (Zeeuws-Vlaanderen, about 3.4–4.0°E, 51.3°N), so occupied fill was drawn over Dutch territory from 1914 to 1918. Every ring now follows the base map's Belgian–Dutch border.

source.title: USMA map 10: Northwest Europe 1914 – German withdrawal to the Aisne and stabilization of the front (Commons)

findings.issue: Western Front had only one position inside the chapter (11 Jul) besides its end, so the German gains at Verdun (Douaumont 25 Feb, Mort-Homme and Côte 304 in March–May, Vaux 2 Jun, Fleury and the Souville high-water mark 23 Jun–11 Jul) and the French recapture (Douaumont 24 Oct, Vaux 2 Nov, Bezonvaux–Côte du Poivre 15–18 Dec) never showed, and the Somme gains appeared as one slide. Added 15 keys from 21 Feb to 18 Dec 1916.

The base map for 1915–1918 gives Germany a fixed slab of northern France that reaches Albert, Arras, Amiens' eastern edge and even Verdun town, so ground the Allies held (Albert behind the British line, Verdun itself) was painted German, and in 1918 the post-Michael bulge was painted German before 21 March and after the Allied advance. Added an Allied-held area that follows the Western Front at every key from Dec 1914 to the armistice, so the map shows the front, not the base map.

source.title: Map of the Battle of the Somme, 1916 (Commons)

findings.issue: Front lines are resampled to 64 points, so Verdun's 2–8 km changes show only faintly at this scale; claims for Verdun use 'on the front' rather than exact holders except for Verdun town itself.
Text did not say how Verdun ended; added that the French had retaken Fort Douaumont and most of the lost ground by December.

Western Front had no position from 29 Apr to 17 Jul, so the Aisne drive to the Marne (27 May–3 Jun) and the Matz offensive (9–12 Jun) slid in over ten weeks instead of days, and Operation Michael (21 Mar–5 Apr) and the Lys offensive (9–29 Apr) shared one interpolation. Added keys on 27 Mar, 5 and 12 Apr, 26 May, 3 and 12 Jun, 14 Jul, 28 Jul and 6 Aug.

source.title: USMA map 18: Western Front 1918 – situation 20 March and the five German offensives to 18 July (Commons)

findings.issue: The chapter stopped on 17 July, before the main event of the Second Battle of the Marne: the Allied counter-offensive from 18 July that pushed the Germans back to the Vesle by 6 August, which no chapter showed. Chapter extended to 6 August, text updated, arrow added.

source.title: Wikipedia: Second Battle of the Marne

findings.issue: The Lys and Matz offensives had no arrows; added. Added battle markers for the Lys and the Third Battle of the Aisne.

Western Front had only one position (25 Sep) between 17 Jul and the armistice, so the Amiens break-in (8–12 Aug), the fall of Albert, Bapaume and Noyon (22–29 Aug), the St-Mihiel attack (12–16 Sep), the Flanders offensive and the liberation of Lille, Ostend and Bruges (17–19 Oct) were one slow slide. Added keys on 6 and 12 Aug, 3, 12 and 16 Sep, 10 and 20 Oct.

source.title: USMA map 23: Western Front 1918 – situation 25 September and Allied advance to 11 November (Commons)

findings.issue: The St-Mihiel salient stayed on the map until 25 September although the Americans and French cut it off on 12–16 September; it now disappears on 16 September, with an arrow and a battle marker.
The armistice line now follows the cited line Terneuzen–Ghent–Scheldt–Ath–Mons–Sivry and the Meuse at Mézières and Sedan.
Laon (liberated 13 Oct 1918) is shown Allied from about 13 Oct by interpolation; no claim added because the fetched source only says 'summer of 1918'.

Outside my chapters: the Western Front slides from the 18 Dec 1916 line to the existing 8 Apr 1917 (Hindenburg Line) key over four months, although the German withdrawal happened on 16–20 March 1917. A hold key about 15 March 1917 would fix it; left for the owner of 1917.

findings.issue: check_history flags 'little visible change' for this chapter (front moves at most about 11 km, net occupied-area change about 100 km²). That is the history: the Somme gained at most about 10 km and the French had regained most of the Verdun ground by December, so the net change is small by design. The movement inside the chapter is now shown by 15 keyframes.

sweep.text: Germany planned to defeat France in about six weeks by swinging through neutral Belgium. Its armies crossed the border on 4 August, which brought Britain into the war, took Liège and Brussels and pushed the French and British back towards Paris, while French offensives into Lorraine and the Ardennes were thrown back.
arrows: German advance through Belgium and France (Schlieffen Plan)

marne.text: French and British counter-attacks on the Marne (5–12 September) forced the Germans back to the Aisne. Each side then tried to get round the other's northern flank in the 'Race to the Sea'; Antwerp fell on 10 October and the Allies held Ypres through a month of fighting. By December a line of trenches ran from the Belgian coast to Switzerland.
arrows: Race to the Sea: German outflanking moves

verdun-somme.text: Germany attacked Verdun in February 1916 to wear down the French army. To relieve it, Britain and France attacked on the Somme on 1 July; the British suffered about 57,000 casualties on the first day alone. Both battles cost hundreds of thousands of lives for a few kilometres of ground, and by December the French had retaken Fort Douaumont and most of the ground lost at Verdun.

spring-1918.text: With troops freed from the east, Germany attacked in the West on 21 March 1918, before American armies could arrive in strength. Its offensives drove deep bulges towards Amiens, across the Lys and down to the Marne by early June, but cost Germany its best troops. A last push over the Marne on 15 July failed, and from 18 July French and American counter-attacks drove the Germans back to the Vesle.
arrows: German spring offensive: Aisne drive to the Marne
